headline: Higgins Beach Blues Find the Bunker, Biddeford Pool Bass Still Running the Incoming
subhead: The bluefish run we called weeks ago is holding at Higgins, but the striper bite up and down the beat is a tide-and-timing game, not a gimme.
body_markdown:
Reports out of Higgins Beach this week point to bluefish working bunker pods just off the third sandbar, and if that sounds familiar, it should — we flagged this pattern back in early August, said wherever bunker concentrate you'd get violent topwater feeds as long as the bait held and the high pressure stayed put. It's holding. The blues at Higgins are running mostly cocktail-to-mid-size class, but there are reports of bigger fish mixed in when the bait balls tighten up on the drop of the tide. A white or bone Gibbs Pencil Popper, worked with a hard walk-the-dog cadence right through the froth, is still the move. Don't be shy about switching to a bunker-colored Hogy Pencil if the blues get finicky on the popper — sometimes it's the subtler wake that seals the deal, especially once the sun climbs and the fish get a little more particular about what they'll chase.

Biddeford Pool remains the best hour of striper fishing on this whole stretch of coast, and that hasn't changed with the calendar. The incoming tide flooding the flats and pushing bait up through the channel is still the window — stripers stack up on that current edge waiting for whatever the tide delivers, and a black or bone Danny plug swung across the seam has been the traditional producer for a reason. Live eels fished on a slow drift through the deeper cuts inside the Pool are worth having rigged as backup, particularly on the tail end of the incoming when the current slows and the fish get more deliberate about what they'll eat. This time of year the bass in the Pool run a mixed bag — plenty of schoolies in the 20-inch class mixed with occasional slot fish pushing 28 to 30 inches, and reports this week suggest that pattern is holding, though nobody's calling it easy. You're better off treating the Pool as a two-tide operation — fish the incoming hard, then reassess rather than grinding it out through a dead high.

Prouts Neck is a different animal entirely, and it lives and dies on wind direction. A southwest wind — which is what's been sitting over the coast this week — pushes bait tight against the rocks and gives the stripers cover to ambush from the boulder fields without getting pushed out into open water. That's when you want a big swimming plug, something like a Danny or a Doc-style swimmer, worked slow and deliberate along the visible structure at first light or last light. The rocks there don't forgive sloppy casting, so if you're new to that stretch, scout it on a lower tide before you try to fish it in the dark. Reports on the size class at Prouts have been modest this week — mostly schoolies working the edges — but the structure is there for something bigger to show up on the right night, and southwest wind is exactly the setup that's produced better fish there in past seasons.

Pine Point is quietly doing what Pine Point does in August — flounder in the channel on incoming water, bloodworms or clam strips fished on a simple two-hook flounder rig, bounced slow along the mud-to-sand transition. It's not glamorous fishing, but it's steady, and it's a good option on a day when the surf's blown out and the bass bite is a coin flip.

Mackerel have thinned out along the piers at Wells Harbor and Ogunquit, which is typical for this point in the summer — the bigger schools have generally pushed offshore and deeper by early August, chasing cooler water and bait. If you're still hoping to jig up mackerel for cut bait or live bait for the bass, your better odds are working the harbor mouths on the early tide before the sun gets high, rather than the open beach fronts.

Cod remain mostly a boat proposition this time of year, working the deeper structure off Cape Elizabeth, and that fishery is out of the surf-plugger's hands — worth a mention for the beat's completeness, but not where the shore-bound crowd should be spending effort in August.

Here's the honest read: this isn't a week where every angler walking the beach is going to load up. The bluefish at Higgins are the most reliable target right now, and that's a direct extension of the bunker pattern we called weeks back — it's holding as long as those pods stay thick and the weather stays settled. The striper bite everywhere else on the beat is real but patchy, tide-dependent, and rewards putting in the hours on the right stage of water rather than showing up whenever and expecting fish. If the southwest wind holds into the coming week, I'd keep Prouts Neck on the short list for a low-light session, and I'd keep working the Biddeford Pool incoming as the anchor of any weekly plan. If the wind swings onshore and stirs things up, shift to Pine Point flounder and treat it as a consolation prize rather than a backup insult — a full stringer of flounder beats an empty plug bag any day of the week.
